narrative: The model estimated a 55.0% chance you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—slightly above a coin flip and high enough to lead to denial of your law school application. That prediction does not mean failure is certain; it means the model saw the balance of evidence leaning toward risk. The strongest factor was your LSAT score of 26, well below the accepted-student average of about 37, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. The second-most influential factor was your high family-income bracket, which pushed toward passing. The third was your undergraduate GPA of 2.80; although it is below the accepted average of about 3.23, it also pushed toward passing. Those positive factors were not enough to offset the LSAT concern. Next, focus on strengthening the weakest signal: prepare for and retake the LSAT if possible, seek admissions advising about schools and application timing, and consider supplemental coursework or a post-baccalaureate record that demonstrates readiness. You may also ask whether a conditional or provisional admission pathway exists.
